body:
ABOUT

FantasyCruncher is a set of tools that were developed for DFS players by DFS players. If you are serious about playing Daily Fantasy, this is the place to be, and you will be in the company of today's top DFS players.

Development of the software started in 2014 and since then has gone on to change the DFS world forever. While others have attempted to replicate, no other software service can come close to offering the multitude of features, the sports & DFS sites supported, the ease of use, the consistent updates, or the customer service we offer.

We are driven by our customers and listen when new features or additions are requested. We have a constant development cycle and will continue to improve and update the software we offer making sure you always have the biggest edge possible playing DFS.

Whether you play on FanDuel, DraftKings, Yahoo or OwnersBox we have you covered and support all the sports including; NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, College Football, College Basketball, GOLF, MMA, NASCAR, SOCCER, WNBA, eSPORTS (League of Legends, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, and Valorant), UFL, CFL, Tennis, F1 and the list keeps growing.

ABOUT

FantasyCruncher is a set of tools that were developed for DFS players by DFS players. If you are serious about playing Daily Fantasy, this is the place to be, and you will be in the company of today's top DFS players.

Development of the software started in 2014 and since then has gone on to change the DFS world forever. While others have attempted to replicate, no other software service can come close to offering the multitude of features, the sports & DFS sites supported, the ease of use, the consistent updates, or the customer service we offer.

We are driven by our customers and listen when new features or additions are requested. We have a constant development cycle and will continue to improve and update the software we offer making sure you always have the biggest edge possible playing DFS.

Whether you play on FanDuel, DraftKings, Yahoo or OwnersBox we have you covered and support all the sports including; NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, College Football, College Basketball, GOLF, MMA, NASCAR, SOCCER, WNBA, eSPORTS (League of Legends, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, and Valorant), UFL, CFL, Tennis, F1 and the list keeps growing.

body:
ABOUT

FantasyCruncher is a set of tools that were developed for DFS players by DFS players. If you are serious about playing Daily Fantasy, this is the place to be, and you will be in the company of today's top DFS players.

Development of the software started in 2014 and since then has gone on to change the DFS world forever. While others have attempted to replicate, no other software service can come close to offering the multitude of features, the sports & DFS sites supported, the ease of use, the consistent updates, or the customer service we offer.

We are driven by our customers and listen when new features or additions are requested. We have a constant development cycle and will continue to improve and update the software we offer making sure you always have the biggest edge possible playing DFS.

Whether you play on FanDuel, DraftKings, Yahoo or OwnersBox we have you covered and support all the sports including; NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, College Football, College Basketball, GOLF, MMA, NASCAR, SOCCER, WNBA, eSPORTS (League of Legends, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, and Valorant), UFL, CFL, Tennis, F1 and the list keeps growing.

fantasycruncher_com_premium.html.txt — part 25/25
body:
ABOUT

FantasyCruncher is a set of tools that were developed for DFS players by DFS players. If you are serious about playing Daily Fantasy, this is the place to be, and you will be in the company of today's top DFS players.

Development of the software started in 2014 and since then has gone on to change the DFS world forever. While others have attempted to replicate, no other software service can come close to offering the multitude of features, the sports & DFS sites supported, the ease of use, the consistent updates, or the customer service we offer.

We are driven by our customers and listen when new features or additions are requested. We have a constant development cycle and will continue to improve and update the software we offer making sure you always have the biggest edge possible playing DFS.

Whether you play on FanDuel, DraftKings, Yahoo or OwnersBox we have you covered and support all the sports including; NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, College Football, College Basketball, GOLF, MMA, NASCAR, SOCCER, WNBA, eSPORTS (League of Legends, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, and Valorant), UFL, CFL, Tennis, F1 and the list keeps growing.

fantasycruncher_com_pricing.html.txt — part 25/25
body:
ABOUT

FantasyCruncher is a set of tools that were developed for DFS players by DFS players. If you are serious about playing Daily Fantasy, this is the place to be, and you will be in the company of today's top DFS players.

Development of the software started in 2014 and since then has gone on to change the DFS world forever. While others have attempted to replicate, no other software service can come close to offering the multitude of features, the sports & DFS sites supported, the ease of use, the consistent updates, or the customer service we offer.

We are driven by our customers and listen when new features or additions are requested. We have a constant development cycle and will continue to improve and update the software we offer making sure you always have the biggest edge possible playing DFS.

Whether you play on FanDuel, DraftKings, Yahoo or OwnersBox we have you covered and support all the sports including; NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, College Football, College Basketball, GOLF, MMA, NASCAR, SOCCER, WNBA, eSPORTS (League of Legends, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, and Valorant), UFL, CFL, Tennis, F1 and the list keeps growing.

body:
ABOUT

FantasyCruncher is a set of tools that were developed for DFS players by DFS players. If you are serious about playing Daily Fantasy, this is the place to be, and you will be in the company of today's top DFS players.

Development of the software started in 2014 and since then has gone on to change the DFS world forever. While others have attempted to replicate, no other software service can come close to offering the multitude of features, the sports & DFS sites supported, the ease of use, the consistent updates, or the customer service we offer.

We are driven by our customers and listen when new features or additions are requested. We have a constant development cycle and will continue to improve and update the software we offer making sure you always have the biggest edge possible playing DFS.

Whether you play on FanDuel, DraftKings, Yahoo or OwnersBox we have you covered and support all the sports including; NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, College Football, College Basketball, GOLF, MMA, NASCAR, SOCCER, WNBA, eSPORTS (League of Legends, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, and Valorant), UFL, CFL, Tennis, F1 and the list keeps growing.

ABOUT

FantasyCruncher is a set of tools that were developed for DFS players by DFS players. If you are serious about playing Daily Fantasy, this is the place to be, and you will be in the company of today's top DFS players.

Development of the software started in 2014 and since then has gone on to change the DFS world forever. While others have attempted to replicate, no other software service can come close to offering the multitude of features, the sports & DFS sites supported, the ease of use, the consistent updates, or the customer service we offer.

We are driven by our customers and listen when new features or additions are requested. We have a constant development cycle and will continue to improve and update the software we offer making sure you always have the biggest edge possible playing DFS.

Whether you play on FanDuel, DraftKings, Yahoo or OwnersBox we have you covered and support all the sports including; NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, College Football, College Basketball, GOLF, MMA, NASCAR, SOCCER, WNBA, eSPORTS (League of Legends, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, and Valorant), UFL, CFL, Tennis, F1 and the list keeps growing.

ABOUT

FantasyCruncher is a set of tools that were developed for DFS players by DFS players. If you are serious about playing Daily Fantasy, this is the place to be, and you will be in the company of today's top DFS players.

Development of the software started in 2014 and since then has gone on to change the DFS world forever. While others have attempted to replicate, no other software service can come close to offering the multitude of features, the sports & DFS sites supported, the ease of use, the consistent updates, or the customer service we offer.

We are driven by our customers and listen when new features or additions are requested. We have a constant development cycle and will continue to improve and update the software we offer making sure you always have the biggest edge possible playing DFS.

Whether you play on FanDuel, DraftKings, Yahoo or OwnersBox we have you covered and support all the sports including; NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, College Football, College Basketball, GOLF, MMA, NASCAR, SOCCER, WNBA, eSPORTS (League of Legends, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, and Valorant), UFL, CFL, Tennis, F1 and the list keeps growing.

<!-- Teardown guard for the stub above. Outside GDPR regions the OneTrust
             SDK stub calls removeTcf(): it deletes window.__tcfapi and the
             __tcfapiLocator iframe, but never removes the message listener the
             TCF stub registered. Running the stub during parse means
             document.body is still null, so its locator iframe is created on a
             5ms retry timer that lands *after* that teardown. The page then
             advertises a locator frame with no __tcfapi behind it: ad iframes
             post __tcfapiCall, the orphaned listener runs, and addToQ throws
             "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'a')" once per call.
             Detach the listener and drop the orphan frame instead of throwing.
             In GDPR regions the SDK installs the real CMP and this guard hands
             the listener back to it. -->
        <script type="text/javascript">
        (function () {
            var stubHandler = window.receiveOTMessage;
            if (typeof stubHandler !== 'function' || typeof window.__tcfapi !== 'function') return;

            function detach() {
                window.removeEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);
                var locator = document.querySelector('iframe[name="__tcfapiLocator"]');
                if (locator && locator.parentNode) locator.parentNode.removeChild(locator);
            }

            // GDPR path: intializeIabStub() overwrites window.receiveOTMessage
            // and registers its own listener without removing the stub's, so
            // both would answer every __tcfapiCall and vendor callbacks could
            // fire twice. Step aside and leave the real CMP's locator frame.
            function yieldToCmp() {
                window.removeEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);
                clearInterval(poll);
            }

            function guardedHandler(event) {
                if (window.receiveOTMessage !== guardedHandler) {
                    yieldToCmp();
                    return;
                }
                if (typeof window.__tcfapi === 'function') {
                    stubHandler(event);
                    return;
                }
                detach();
            }

            window.removeEventListener('message', stubHandler, false);
            window.receiveOTMessage = guardedHandler;
            window.addEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);

            // Vendors that already saw the locator frame wait for a reply that
            // can no longer come, so drop it as soon as the SDK has decided
            // rather than on the first message.
            //
            // Two consecutive misses, not one: today's SDK only assigns
            // __tcfapi when it is undefined and never deletes it on the GDPR
            // path, but it is remote code, and a single sample landing in a
            // future delete-then-reinstall gap would strip a live CMP's
            // locator frame. detach() is idempotent and the interval keeps
            // running, so a frame created by the stub's own pending
            // addFrame() retry after the teardown gets cleaned up too.
            var checks = 0;
            var misses = 0;
            var poll = setInterval(function () {
                if (window.receiveOTMessage !== guardedHandler) {
                    yieldToCmp();
                    return;
                }
                if (typeof window.__tcfapi === 'function') {
                    misses = 0;
                } else if (++misses > 1) {
                    detach();
                }
                if (++checks > 80) clearInterval(poll);
            }, 250);
        })();
        </script>

        <script type="text/javascript">
            function OptanonWrapper() {

                window.fpGetCookieGeoInfo = function() {
                    let geoInfo = {
                        isCCPA: false,
                        isGDPR: false,
                    };

                    const oneTrustGeo = window.OneTrust?.getGeolocationData();
                    const fpGdpr = FP?.readCookie('fpisgdpr');
                    const fpState = FP?.readCookie('fpdefloc');

                    // getGeolocationData() returns an ISO country code ('DE'), never 'EU',
                    // so ask OneTrust which template it applied instead: only the EU and UK
                    // rules use the IAB TCF template. That signal is ready on the first
                    // pageview, while `fpisgdpr` only exists after api/nc/defloc.php has run.
                    const oneTrustIsTcf = window.OneTrust?.GetDomainData?.()?.IabType === 'IAB2V2';

                    if (fpGdpr || oneTrustIsTcf) {
                        geoInfo.isGDPR = true;
                    }
                    if (fpState === 'CA' || (oneTrustGeo?.state === 'CA' && oneTrustGeo?.country === 'US')) {
                        geoInfo.isCCPA = true;
                    }

                    return geoInfo;
                }

                window.fpSetCookieOptout = function(groupsToCheck = []) {
                    if (!groupsToCheck || !groupsToCheck.length) return;

                    const targetedCookieGroups = ['C0002', 'C0004'];
                    let isOptedout = false;
                    targetedCookieGroups.forEach(group => {
                        if (!groupsToCheck.includes(group)) {
                            isOptedout = true;
                        }
                    });

                    window.fpCookieOptout = isOptedout;
                    if (isOptedout && !FP?.readCookie('_pbjs_id_optout') && (window?.fpCookieGeoInfo?.isGDPR || window?.fpCookieGeoInfo?.isCCPA)) {
                        // user is opted - prevents userId modules from firing
                        FP?.createCookie('_pbjs_id_optout', '1', 365);
                    }
                }

                window.fpOptoutCookieGroups = ['C0002', 'C0004'];
                window.fpCookieOptout = window.fpCookieOptout || false;
                window.fpCookieGeoInfo = window.fpCookieGeoInfo || window.fpGetCookieGeoInfo();

                if (!window.fpCookieOptout && window?.OnetrustActiveGroups) {
                    const activeGroups = window.OnetrustActiveGroups?.split(',');
                    if (activeGroups?.length) {
                        window.fpSetCookieOptout(activeGroups);
                    }
                }

<!-- Teardown guard for the stub above. Outside GDPR regions the OneTrust
             SDK stub calls removeTcf(): it deletes window.__tcfapi and the
             __tcfapiLocator iframe, but never removes the message listener the
             TCF stub registered. Running the stub during parse means
             document.body is still null, so its locator iframe is created on a
             5ms retry timer that lands *after* that teardown. The page then
             advertises a locator frame with no __tcfapi behind it: ad iframes
             post __tcfapiCall, the orphaned listener runs, and addToQ throws
             "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'a')" once per call.
             Detach the listener and drop the orphan frame instead of throwing.
             In GDPR regions the SDK installs the real CMP and this guard hands
             the listener back to it. -->
        <script type="text/javascript">
        (function () {
            var stubHandler = window.receiveOTMessage;
            if (typeof stubHandler !== 'function' || typeof window.__tcfapi !== 'function') return;

            function detach() {
                window.removeEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);
                var locator = document.querySelector('iframe[name="__tcfapiLocator"]');
                if (locator && locator.parentNode) locator.parentNode.removeChild(locator);
            }

            // GDPR path: intializeIabStub() overwrites window.receiveOTMessage
            // and registers its own listener without removing the stub's, so
            // both would answer every __tcfapiCall and vendor callbacks could
            // fire twice. Step aside and leave the real CMP's locator frame.
            function yieldToCmp() {
                window.removeEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);
                clearInterval(poll);
            }

            function guardedHandler(event) {
                if (window.receiveOTMessage !== guardedHandler) {
                    yieldToCmp();
                    return;
                }
                if (typeof window.__tcfapi === 'function') {
                    stubHandler(event);
                    return;
                }
                detach();
            }

            window.removeEventListener('message', stubHandler, false);
            window.receiveOTMessage = guardedHandler;
            window.addEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);

            // Vendors that already saw the locator frame wait for a reply that
            // can no longer come, so drop it as soon as the SDK has decided
            // rather than on the first message.
            //
            // Two consecutive misses, not one: today's SDK only assigns
            // __tcfapi when it is undefined and never deletes it on the GDPR
            // path, but it is remote code, and a single sample landing in a
            // future delete-then-reinstall gap would strip a live CMP's
            // locator frame. detach() is idempotent and the interval keeps
            // running, so a frame created by the stub's own pending
            // addFrame() retry after the teardown gets cleaned up too.
            var checks = 0;
            var misses = 0;
            var poll = setInterval(function () {
                if (window.receiveOTMessage !== guardedHandler) {
                    yieldToCmp();
                    return;
                }
                if (typeof window.__tcfapi === 'function') {
                    misses = 0;
                } else if (++misses > 1) {
                    detach();
                }
                if (++checks > 80) clearInterval(poll);
            }, 250);
        })();
        </script>

        <!-- OneTrust Cookies Consent Notice start -->
        <script async src="https://cdn.cookielaw.org/consent/042af040-2d8c-401b-961f-8d39045cf0aa/otSDKStub.js"  type="text/javascript" charset="UTF-8" data-domain-script="042af040-2d8c-401b-961f-8d39045cf0aa" ></script>
        <script type="text/javascript">
            function OptanonWrapper() {

                window.fpGetCookieGeoInfo = function() {
                    let geoInfo = {
                        isCCPA: false,
                        isGDPR: false,
                    };

                    const oneTrustGeo = window.OneTrust?.getGeolocationData();
                    const fpGdpr = FP?.readCookie('fpisgdpr');
                    const fpState = FP?.readCookie('fpdefloc');

                    // getGeolocationData() returns an ISO country code ('DE'), never 'EU',
                    // so ask OneTrust which template it applied instead: only the EU and UK
                    // rules use the IAB TCF template. That signal is ready on the first
                    // pageview, while `fpisgdpr` only exists after api/nc/defloc.php has run.
                    const oneTrustIsTcf = window.OneTrust?.GetDomainData?.()?.IabType === 'IAB2V2';

                    if (fpGdpr || oneTrustIsTcf) {
                        geoInfo.isGDPR = true;
                    }
                    if (fpState === 'CA' || (oneTrustGeo?.state === 'CA' && oneTrustGeo?.country === 'US')) {
                        geoInfo.isCCPA = true;
                    }

                    return geoInfo;
                }

                window.fpSetCookieOptout = function(groupsToCheck = []) {
                    if (!groupsToCheck || !groupsToCheck.length) return;

                    const targetedCookieGroups = ['C0002', 'C0004'];
                    let isOptedout = false;
                    targetedCookieGroups.forEach(group => {
                        if (!groupsToCheck.includes(group)) {
                            isOptedout = true;
                        }
                    });

                    window.fpCookieOptout = isOptedout;
                    if (isOptedout && !FP?.readCookie('_pbjs_id_optout') && (window?.fpCookieGeoInfo?.isGDPR || window?.fpCookieGeoInfo?.isCCPA)) {
                        // user is opted - prevents userId modules from firing
                        FP?.createCookie('_pbjs_id_optout', '1', 365);
                    }
                }

                window.fpOptoutCookieGroups = ['C0002', 'C0004'];
                window.fpCookieOptout = window.fpCookieOptout || false;
                window.fpCookieGeoInfo = window.fpCookieGeoInfo || window.fpGetCookieGeoInfo();

                if (!window.fpCookieOptout && window?.OnetrustActiveGroups) {
                    const activeGroups = window.OnetrustActiveGroups?.split(',');
                    if (activeGroups?.length) {
                        window.fpSetCookieOptout(activeGroups);
                    }
                }

<!-- Teardown guard for the stub above. Outside GDPR regions the OneTrust
             SDK stub calls removeTcf(): it deletes window.__tcfapi and the
             __tcfapiLocator iframe, but never removes the message listener the
             TCF stub registered. Running the stub during parse means
             document.body is still null, so its locator iframe is created on a
             5ms retry timer that lands *after* that teardown. The page then
             advertises a locator frame with no __tcfapi behind it: ad iframes
             post __tcfapiCall, the orphaned listener runs, and addToQ throws
             "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'a')" once per call.
             Detach the listener and drop the orphan frame instead of throwing.
             In GDPR regions the SDK installs the real CMP and this guard hands
             the listener back to it. -->
        <script type="text/javascript">
        (function () {
            var stubHandler = window.receiveOTMessage;
            if (typeof stubHandler !== 'function' || typeof window.__tcfapi !== 'function') return;

            function detach() {
                window.removeEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);
                var locator = document.querySelector('iframe[name="__tcfapiLocator"]');
                if (locator && locator.parentNode) locator.parentNode.removeChild(locator);
            }

            // GDPR path: intializeIabStub() overwrites window.receiveOTMessage
            // and registers its own listener without removing the stub's, so
            // both would answer every __tcfapiCall and vendor callbacks could
            // fire twice. Step aside and leave the real CMP's locator frame.
            function yieldToCmp() {
                window.removeEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);
                clearInterval(poll);
            }

            function guardedHandler(event) {
                if (window.receiveOTMessage !== guardedHandler) {
                    yieldToCmp();
                    return;
                }
                if (typeof window.__tcfapi === 'function') {
                    stubHandler(event);
                    return;
                }
                detach();
            }

            window.removeEventListener('message', stubHandler, false);
            window.receiveOTMessage = guardedHandler;
            window.addEventListener('message', guardedHandler, false);

            // Vendors that already saw the locator frame wait for a reply that
            // can no longer come, so drop it as soon as the SDK has decided
            // rather than on the first message.
            //
            // Two consecutive misses, not one: today's SDK only assigns
            // __tcfapi when it is undefined and never deletes it on the GDPR
            // path, but it is remote code, and a single sample landing in a
            // future delete-then-reinstall gap would strip a live CMP's
            // locator frame. detach() is idempotent and the interval keeps
            // running, so a frame created by the stub's own pending
            // addFrame() retry after the teardown gets cleaned up too.
            var checks = 0;
            var misses = 0;
            var poll = setInterval(function () {
                if (window.receiveOTMessage !== guardedHandler) {
                    yieldToCmp();
                    return;
                }
                if (typeof window.__tcfapi === 'function') {
                    misses = 0;
                } else if (++misses > 1) {
                    detach();
                }
                if (++checks > 80) clearInterval(poll);
            }, 250);
        })();
        </script>

            function OptanonWrapper() {

                window.fpGetCookieGeoInfo = function() {
                    let geoInfo = {
                        isCCPA: false,
                        isGDPR: false,
                    };

                    const oneTrustGeo = window.OneTrust?.getGeolocationData();
                    const fpGdpr = FP?.readCookie('fpisgdpr');
                    const fpState = FP?.readCookie('fpdefloc');

                    // getGeolocationData() returns an ISO country code ('DE'), never 'EU',
                    // so ask OneTrust which template it applied instead: only the EU and UK
                    // rules use the IAB TCF template. That signal is ready on the first
                    // pageview, while `fpisgdpr` only exists after api/nc/defloc.php has run.
                    const oneTrustIsTcf = window.OneTrust?.GetDomainData?.()?.IabType === 'IAB2V2';

                    if (fpGdpr || oneTrustIsTcf) {
                        geoInfo.isGDPR = true;
                    }
                    if (fpState === 'CA' || (oneTrustGeo?.state === 'CA' && oneTrustGeo?.country === 'US')) {
                        geoInfo.isCCPA = true;
                    }

                    return geoInfo;
                }

                window.fpSetCookieOptout = function(groupsToCheck = []) {
                    if (!groupsToCheck || !groupsToCheck.length) return;

                    const targetedCookieGroups = ['C0002', 'C0004'];
                    let isOptedout = false;
                    targetedCookieGroups.forEach(group => {
                        if (!groupsToCheck.includes(group)) {
                            isOptedout = true;
                        }
                    });

                    window.fpCookieOptout = isOptedout;
                    if (isOptedout && !FP?.readCookie('_pbjs_id_optout') && (window?.fpCookieGeoInfo?.isGDPR || window?.fpCookieGeoInfo?.isCCPA)) {
                        // user is opted - prevents userId modules from firing
                        FP?.createCookie('_pbjs_id_optout', '1', 365);
                    }
                }

                window.fpOptoutCookieGroups = ['C0002', 'C0004'];
                window.fpCookieOptout = window.fpCookieOptout || false;
                window.fpCookieGeoInfo = window.fpCookieGeoInfo || window.fpGetCookieGeoInfo();

                if (!window.fpCookieOptout && window?.OnetrustActiveGroups) {
                    const activeGroups = window.OnetrustActiveGroups?.split(',');
                    if (activeGroups?.length) {
                        window.fpSetCookieOptout(activeGroups);
                    }
                }

Frequently Asked Questions

 What is a prop betting model?
 
A prop betting model is an algorithm that projects a player's statistical output - passing yards, points, rebounds, strikeouts - and compares that projection to the sportsbook's line. When the model's projection differs meaningfully from the line, the bet has positive expected value (+EV). Our model runs these projections automatically for every NFL, NBA, and MLB player prop and ranks the board by edge, so you see the most mispriced lines first.
 How do your NFL player prop picks work?
 
Our NFL projection model accounts for matchup quality, pace, weather, injuries, and usage trends to project every player's stat line each week. We compare those projections against live lines from DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM, and Caesars and rank every prop by edge percentage. The board updates as lines move, and covers gameday props plus season-long player and team props.
 What is a DFS lineup optimizer?
 
A DFS lineup optimizer uses algorithms to build mathematically optimal daily fantasy sports lineups for DraftKings, FanDuel, and Yahoo. It factors in player projections, salary caps, ownership percentages, stacking correlations, and roster constraints to generate lineups that maximize expected value for both cash games and GPP tournaments.
 How does the Fantasy Team Advice DFS optimizer work?
 
Our optimizer ingests real-time player projections, ownership percentages, Vegas totals, injury reports, and starting lineup confirmations. You set stacking rules, player exposure limits, and contest type - cash or GPP - and the engine generates up to 150 salary-cap-compliant lineups in seconds. Every lineup is built to maximize projected points while balancing ownership leverage.
 Can the optimizer build my DFS lineups automatically?
 
Yes. Set your contest type (cash or GPP), stacking rules, and exposure limits once - the optimizer generates up to 150 salary-cap-compliant DraftKings, FanDuel, or Yahoo lineups in seconds and exports them as a CSV you can upload directly to your contests. Projections, ownership, Vegas totals, and late injury news are already baked in.
 What sports does the model cover?
 
NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL. During NFL season you get weekly prop projections, gameday and season-long prop pages, and full DFS optimizer support for DraftKings, FanDuel, and Yahoo.  Are your player prop tools useful for prediction markets, not just sportsbooks?
 
Yes. Our projections, edge percentages, and hit-rate tracking are built around the underlying player performance, not a specific sportsbook's odds format - so they work whether you're betting a sportsbook prop or trading a player-performance contract on a prediction market. Compare our projected stat line against whatever line or contract price you're evaluating to find your edge.

    FantasyCruncher

    August 1, 2019 by

    Fantasy Cruncher Review – Factoid Style Bits of Info and Opinion on FantasyCruncher

    What is FantasyCruncher?

    Fantasy Cruncher is a DFS tool that lets you create multiple optimized lineups for the big DFS sites. They call it their ‘Lineup Cruncher’.

    They work for all the major sports and at the big DFS sites.

    The biggest thing they have is their ‘lineup cruncher’. It lets you build and optimize mass entry lineups. You can tweak projections, like or dislike players, create any stacking rules you want and FC will make the lineups fit. FC will also put together dozens and dozens optimized lineups based on your input. It’s user friendly with thumbs up and downs on players.

    It was built organically as a tool a DFS player needed himself and opened up to the Reddit DFS community.

    You use it by tweaking the projections for players. Set the guys you like to higher points projected and lower for the guys you don’t like. FC does the rest.

    FantasyCruncher puts together optimized lineups for mass entry players. It’s been called a must have for employing the mass entry strategy to win the big GPP. You want to drop 100 lineups in the quarter arcade? It’s by far the best tool for the job.

    Is it worth it? Up to you, of course.

    How Much does Fantasy Cruncher Cost?

There are two different plans that can be purchased by the week, the month, or the year. They are called a “Premium” plan and a “Pro” plan.

The price for the “Premium” plan is

  • $19.95 weekly
  • $59.95 monthly
  • $599.95 yearly

and that includes the following

  • Full access to line-up cruncher
  • Access to FC’s insight premium content
  • Access to line-up rewind with user saved data

For the “Pro plan, the price is as follows

  • $39.90 weekly
  • $119.90 monthly
  • $1199.90 yearly

and you get all of the features that come in the Premium plan, plus

  • Access to line-up study
  • Projected ownership from Awesemo
  • Additional software enhancements to Lineup Cruncher

If you aren’t sure you can try it for a week or an month and cancel if you want. It’s easy to do so. If you like the tool and think it is worth it then by all means, giddyup.

Using Fantasy Crunchers DFS tool the ‘Lineup Cruncher’

They make liking/disliking players, building stacks, adding some custom rules easy. There are an absolute ton of advanced options you can use too, such as, set how many unique players per lineup keeping your lineups varied but optimized or set how many players max / min from each game every week.

If you play GPP’s with a lot of lineups then this tool will work for you.

It was super easy exporting lineups into Draftkings, even my technically challenged self could do it. I put 20 FantasyCruncher optimized lineups into the quarter arcade and one lineup I built myself without the optimizer.

The FC lineups crushed my personal lineup. I had Derrick Carr as my QB and he sucked it up. Of course it was only one lineup but we’ve got anecdotal evidence up in here.

There are a lot of advanced features you can use to build your team out.

Position stacks – like QB paired with one WR from the same team.

Team stacks where you can add players from opposing teams. So if you think it’s going to be a shootout then snag players from both sides and hope for the huge points stack. You can add groups of players that let you fine tune your lineups to work certain pairings of players together.

You can work on your lineups as much or as little as you want. The projections they have are from their pro’s but you should tweak them to what you think.

You pick some players you think are going to crush it or who aren’t likely to reach their ceiling and adjust your like/dislike and their projections.

You put together all these rules and features and build mass lineups. You mass enter GPP’s with optimized, varied multiple lineups and start praying to the DFS gods that one of them takes it down. You can see defense V position on the players tab.

You can see how many points Vegas thinks each team is going to score.

You can sort by 15 different factors.

There are different fields for Fantasy Crunchers projections and a a field for your own projections if you want to make them different.

You can adjust your exposure settings to individual players if you want for max exposure when considering the player for the lineups.

You can add up to three ‘thumbs ups’ and ‘ thumbs down’ to a player which affects how highly that player is considered in the lineup.

You can lock players in and out of lineups.

Likes and dislikes for players.

You can build a ton of lineups and then tweak them all from there by clicking on the player you want more or less exposure to and adjust it. Then, recalculate.

When you build a stacking rule you have to click the ‘add stacking rule’ button to apply it to your lineups.

When building your lineups you can adjust players and percentages they are used in your lineups pretty easily.

The systems builds the lineups really fast. 20 lineups is built in 10-20 seconds and the first ones start displaying withing a second or two of calculating. This might be a little slower if you are doing this on Sunday mornings.

You can build lineups for Draftkings, Fanduel, FantasyDraft and Yahoo!.

When you roll over the injured tag next to a player the injury info pops up automatically without having to click. I like that.

Share, trash, save and download your lineups and or lineup easily.

If you build your projections yourself and want to upload them, they have a tool for that.

NFL, NBA, PGA, NAS, NHL, MLB, EURO Golf, CFL, MMA and even WNBA are supported with their lineup cruncher.

Is Fantasy Cruncher Legit? Yes.

Yes, buy it and try it if you want. Cancel anytime.

They have maintained a positive reputation with their clients.

They’ve been easy to work with from me as an affiliate and paid smoothly.

Try it for a week, it’s $19.95 to use the lineup cruncher.

FantasyCruncher: The Original DFS Lineup Optimizer That Still Delivers

Introduction

When it comes to Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS) lineup optimizers, FantasyCruncher stands as one of the original and most widely used tools in the industry. Long before many DFS platforms incorporated advanced simulation models and ownership projections, FantasyCruncher was helping DFS players build high-quality, data-driven lineups with its intuitive optimizer and extensive customization features.

While some may critique the leadership and customer service reputation of FantasyCruncher, there’s no denying its track record of success. Many of the biggest DFS winners on DraftKings and FanDuel have used FantasyCruncher to power their lineups, and it remains a staple for serious DFS players who prioritize a powerful, time-tested optimizer over fancy bells and whistles.

Key Features of FantasyCruncher

1. The Industry’s First & Most Used DFS Lineup Optimizer

At its core, FantasyCruncher is built around its optimizer, which allows users to create hundreds or even thousands of DFS lineups in minutes.

🔥 Mass Multi-Entry (MME) Capabilities – Whether you’re building 5, 20, or 150 lineups, FantasyCruncher lets you generate optimized lineups at scale with ease.
📊 Advanced Customization – Users can set player exposures, lock in core plays, and exclude bad chalk to create high-upside, unique lineup constructions.
⚡ Lightning-Fast Processing – Unlike some competitors with clunky and slow optimizers, FantasyCruncher is known for its speed and efficiency.

2. Custom Projections & Aggregation Tools

One of FantasyCruncher’s biggest strengths is its ability to import and customize projections.

✅ Upload Your Own Projections – Users can input their own data or merge multiple projection sources.
🔄 Weighted Projection Averages – Blend multiple projection sets to create a balanced, data-driven approach.
📈 Ownership & Value Projections – While not as sophisticated as some newer competitors, FantasyCruncher still offers solid ownership and value insights.

3. Rules, Stacking & Correlation Settings for Maximum Control

For DFS tournament players, FantasyCruncher provides some of the best stacking and correlation settings in the industry.

🔗 Team & Positional Stacking – Easily create QB-WR stacks for NFL, game stacks for NBA, or team stacks for MLB.
🎯 Position & Player Grouping Rules – Avoid negative correlations by setting conditional rules (e.g., “Never pair two RBs from the same team”).
🔄 Min & Max Exposure Limits – Control how diversified or concentrated your lineups are for large-field GPPs.

4. Late Swap Optimizer for Adjusting Lineups in Real Time

FantasyCruncher offers a Late Swap Tool, which helps adjust lineups based on injury news or unexpected scratches.

🚨 Real-Time Updates – Quickly adjust lineups before lock without starting over.
✅ Minimize Dead Lineups – Ensure your contests stay competitive even after late-breaking news.

How FantasyCruncher Helps Different Types of DFS Players

For DFS Tournament Players (GPPs & MME)

🏆 Perfect for Multi-Entry Players – FantasyCruncher is one of the best tools for players who enter 20+ lineups into contests.
📊 Strong Customization & Stacking Features – Allows for highly controlled and strategic lineup constructions.
🔥 Highly Used by Pros & High-Stakes Players – Many biggest DFS winners rely on FantasyCruncher for their process.

For Cash Game & Single-Entry DFS Players

✅ Solid Projections & Optimized Lineups – Helps identify the best plays for head-to-head and double-up contests.
🚀 Time-Saving Tool – Even if you’re only building a few lineups, FantasyCruncher streamlines the process.

The FantasyCruncher Reputation: A Mixed Bag

While FantasyCruncher is one of the most respected tools in the DFS space, its leadership and customer service reputation has been a point of contention for some users.

    Jeff Ratcliffe

    Jeff Ratcliffe is a fantasy and betting analyst who specializes in football and basketball, along with dabbling in NASCAR and Horse Racing.
    Aaron Schatz

    Aaron Schatz has been doing NFL analytics for over 20 years and is the creator of advanced stats including DVOA, DYAR, and Adjusted Line Yards. He also writes for ESPN+ and ESPN Bet and hosts the FTN Fantasy Schatz and Tanier NFL Podcast. He is also one of the 50 members of the Associated Press NFL voting panel for regular-season awards and the All-Pro team.
    Tyler Orginski

    Tyler has been playing fantasy football for over 20 years and been creating FF content for seven. When not fighting for his life in the spreadsheets, he enjoys spending time with his family and playing video games. Tyler won the Fantasy Pros 2024 Accuracy Contest. The secret? Many are saying he’s never watched a game.
    Vlad Sedler

    Vlad is the head of fantasy baseball content at FTN Fantasy. He also writes for FanGraphs, is a Tout Wars Expert League champ, member of the CDM Fantasy Sports Hall of Fame and has been nominated for FSWA writing awards six times. Vlad has been playing fantasy baseball since 1995, winning 42 NFBC leagues since 2012 and ranking in the top percentile in NFBC’s Online Championship contest (33% win rate, 52% cash rate; 64 leagues). Much to the chagrin of his colleagues and most baseball aficionados, Vlad is a lifelong Dodgers fan who claims his first gut call at age 9 was Kirk Gibson’s 1988 World Series home run. Some, but not all, call him the FAAB Whisperer.
    Tyler Loechner

    Tyler is a 20-year fantasy football vet specializing in redraft, DFS, best ball, and dynasty. He has earned multiple FSWA nominations and won the Best Football Series award in 2017. Tyler previously wrote for PFF Fantasy, RotoViz, and Bleacher Report.
    Frank Brank

    Frank Brank is a former college baseball pitcher and professional sports bettor who brings a data-driven, market-focused approach to sports analysis. With years of experience building predictive betting models and consistently beating the market across all major sports, Frank specializes in identifying value, interpreting line movement, and turning advanced analytics into actionable betting insights. His background as an athlete gives him a unique understanding of game flow, player performance, and competitive dynamics, while his success as a professional gambler allows him to break down betting markets with a sharp, numbers-first perspective.

We're concerned about problem gambling. For most people, gambling is entertainment - a fun activity that can be enjoyed without harmful effect. But for some, it's not just a game - it's a serious problem that continues even after the fun has gone.

Compulsive gambling is not easily detected. The person with a gambling problem will often go to great lengths to cover up the problem and will appear to look all right, regardless of the consequences of their gambling.

Warning Signs. Some of the indicators that a person may be suffering from a gambling problem include:


  • Losing time from work or family due to gambling.
  • Repeated failed attempts to stop or control gambling.
  • Borrowing money to gamble or pay gambling debts.
  • Gambling to escape worry or trouble.
  • Neglecting the care of one's self or family in order to gamble.
  • Lying about the amount of time and money spent on gambling.
  • Gambling more money in an attempt to win back losses.
  • Selling or pawning personal possessions to get money to gamble.

OverviewGetting StartedAPI Reference

PredictionData Markets API

The PredictionData API provides direct access to high-quality, normalized sportsbook markets and reference data. Our feed powers pricing models, trading tools, market monitoring, and internal analytics workflows across major North American leagues and leading global soccer competitions.

Data Delivery Modes

Pull API

The Pull API is ideal for retrieving the latest markets snapshot whenever you need it. Use it for:

Use cases:

  • Scheduled polling (e.g., every few seconds/minutes)
  • On-demand pricing or modeling workflows
  • Backfilling and reconciling internal datasets

Markets Stream (SSE)

The Markets Stream delivers real-time pricing updates over Server-Sent Events (SSE). It's designed for:

Use cases:

  • Live market-movement tracking
  • Trading interfaces and alerting systems
  • Low-latency models that react to odds changes

Core Endpoints

GET

/markets

Retrieve markets filtered by league, book, bet type, period, and more.

Supported Market Types:

MoneylinesSpreadsTotalsPropsFutures

Filters:

  • Live/pre-game filters
  • Alternate lines support

Reference Data Endpoints

Access comprehensive reference data for players, teams, fixtures, and seasons.

"labels": [], "state": "open", "locked": false, "assignees": [], "milestone": null, "comments": 1, "created_at": "2026-07-17T02:14:33Z", "updated_at": "2026-07-25T05:12:56Z", "closed_at": null, "assignee": null, "author_association": "NONE", "issue_field_values": [], "type": null, "active_lock_reason": null, "sub_issues_summary": { "total": 0, "completed": 0, "percent_completed": 0 }, "issue_dependencies_summary": { "blocked_by": 0, "total_blocked_by": 0, "blocking": 0, "total_blocking": 0 }, "body": "## Summary When both teams have no observed player coordinates for a retained frame, `DiscreteVoronoiModel` preserves an all-`NaN` internal ownership grid, but its public aggregation methods return finite numeric values: - every player: `0.0` - Home: `0.0` - Away: `0.0` This converts: ```text no territorial-control observation exists ``` into: ```text an observed territorial-control value of zero ``` I would like maintainer guidance on treating this state as missing before preparing a production PR. The proposed initial repair is intentionally narrow: preserve temporal alignment and return `NaN` for player and team control only when the internal ownership frame contains no assigned owner. During reproduction, I also found broader observation-validity questions around one-team dropout, partial-player dropout, and motion-model derivative support. Those findings are documented below so that the narrow scope is an explicit design decision rather than an omission. --- ## Minimal reproduction ```python import numpy as np from floodlight import Pitch, XY from floodlight.models.space import DiscreteVoronoiModel pitch = Pitch.from_template("dfl", length=105, width=68, sport="football") missing_home = XY(np.full((3, 2), np.nan), framerate=10) missing_away = XY(np.full((3, 2), np.nan), framerate=10) model = DiscreteVoronoiModel( pitch, mesh="square", xpoints=10, motion_model="euclidean", ) model.fit(missing_home, missing_away) print(np.all(np.isnan(model._cell_controls_))) # True print(model.player_controls()[0].property) # currently [[0.], [0.], [0.]] print(model.team_controls()[0].property) # currently [[0.], [0.], [0.]] ``` The same public `0.0` behavior was reproduced for: - Euclidean ownership - Taki–Hasegawa ownership - Fujimura–Sugihara ownership - square meshes - hexagonal meshes --- ## Current mathematical behavior Let `G` be all mesh cells, `o_t(g)` the owner stored for cell `g` at frame `t`, `N_H` the number of Home players, and `i` a stacked player identifier. The current player aggregation is: ```text C_i(t) = round(100 * count(o_t(g) == i) / |G|, 2) ``` The current team aggregation is: ```text C_H(t) = round(100 * count(o_t(g) < N_H) / |G|, 2) C_A(t) = round(100 * count(o_t(g) >= N_H) / |G|, 2) ``` The denominator is always the total number of grid cells. For a completely unobserved frame, the producer retains an all-`NaN` ownership grid. Comparisons involving `NaN` are false, so every numerator is zero while the denominator remains nonzero: ```text 100 * 0 / |G| = 0 ``` The resulting `0.0` is therefore produced by aggregation mechanics rather than by an observed territorial partition. --- ## Shared architectural impact All supported configurations converge on the same internal ownership array and the same public aggregation boundary: ```text Home/Away XY inputs ↓ Euclidean, Taki–Hasegawa, or Fujimura–Sugihara costs ↓ square or hexagonal mesh ownership ↓ _cell_controls_ ↓ player_controls() team_controls() ``` The ownership producer already preserves the fully undefined state correctly as an all-`NaN` frame. Semantic information is lost only when `player_controls()` and `team_controls()` convert that frame into percentages. This means the defect affects every model/mesh path but has one shared, surgical repair boundary. --- ## Why this matters A finite zero normally communicates that a quantity was observed and measured as zero. That is not the state represented here: no ownership observation exists. The distinction matters for temporal averages, tactical summaries, frame-wise comparisons, downstream statistics, missing-data filtering, plotting, and reporting. The frame should remain present so temporal alignment is preserved. Its numerical output should communicate that the estimate is undefined. This is consistent with Floodlight's existing use of `NaN` in property, geometry, resampling, plotting, and aggregation workflows. --- ## Controlled reproduction and dropout-sensitivity experiment A deterministic synthetic experiment compared dropout-perturbed outputs with complete-data outputs from the same trajectories and model configuration. The experiment included: - 78 complete-data references - 2,220 deterministic dropout cases - 28,032 frame-level results - 0 failed cases - 0 nonfatal warnings - all three ownership models - both mesh types - representative mesh resolutions at `xpoints=10`, `20`, and `40` - six static formation families - three dynamic trajectory families - exact clean-process reproducibility These are implementation-specific synthetic sensitivity results. They do not establish real-world model accuracy, provider-wide dropout behavior, or a universal acceptable-error threshold.
Principal observation-validity findings ### Both teams fully unobserved Every tested path produced: ```text finite owner cells = 0 internal ownership = all NaN public player outputs = 0.0 public team outputs = 0.0 / 0.0 ``` This state is categorically non-estimable. ### One complete team unobserved Current output becomes a conserved `100/0` or `0/100` partition. Against matched complete-data references, maximum team-control error ranged from `36.25` to `63.46` percentage points. A numerically conserved 100% partition therefore does not establish that the observation is scientifically complete. ### Partial-player dropout When at least one player remains observed for each team, Floodlight partitions the pitch among the remaining players. The resulting estimand is territorial control conditional on the observed players. Across tested partial-dropout cases with both teams still represented: ```text maximum team error range: 0.00 to 60.38 percentage points leave-one-player-out maximum: 8.46 percentage points matched random-subset maximum: 22.19 percentage points ``` At identical 87.5% player coverage, different missing-player identities produced `0.00` versus `6.92` percentage-point team error. Player count or observed fraction is descriptive but cannot determine error by itself. ### Owned-cell coverage Whenever any valid player remained, the current producer assigned every grid cell, so `owned_cell_fraction = 1.0`. Only a completely unobserved frame produced `owned_cell_fraction = 0.0`. Owned-cell fraction therefore measures whether the algorithm produced any partition, not whether the tracking observation was complete. ### Motion-model temporal support Euclidean ownership remained frame-local. Taki–Hasegawa and Fujimura–Sugihara use velocity preprocessing based on neighboring frames. Missing intervals affected one otherwise position-observed frame immediately before and one immediately after the interval in the tested implementation. Position presence and derivative support are therefore separate validity dimensions.
--- ## Observation states uncovered by the investigation | Observation state | Current public behavior | Interpretation | |---|---|---| | Fully observed | Current percentages | Complete-data model estimate | | Partial Home dropout | Conserved conditional repartition | Conditional on observed Home players | | Partial Away dropout | Conserved conditional repartition | Conditional on observed Away players | | Partial bilateral dropout | Conserved conditional repartition | Conditional on both observed subsets | | Home entirely unobserved | `0/100` | Away-only partition | | Away entirely unobserved | `100/0` | Home-only partition | | Both teams entirely unobserved | `0/0` | No estimable ownership observation | | Motion-neighbor affected | Finite percentages | Positions present, derivative support affected | The proposed initial repair addresses only the categorically unambiguous aggregation defect: ```text both teams fully unobserved → no assigned owner exists → return NaN ``` The other states require broader policy or API design. --- ## Recommended initial repair: no-owner `NaN` guard A disposable local prototype used one private shared predicate derived directly from the existing ownership grid: ```python def _frames_have_assigned_owners(self) -> np.ndarray: return np.any(np.isfinite(self._cell_controls_), axis=(1, 2)) ``` Both `player_controls()` and `team_controls()` use the same predicate after their existing percentage calculations. The predicate name intentionally states only that an owner exists. It does not claim that the frame is fully observed, scientifically complete, or valid for every analytical purpose. ### Proposed semantics | Internal ownership state | Proposed public behavior | |---|---| | At least one assigned owner | Preserve all current percentages exactly | | No assigned owner | Every retained player and both teams become `NaN` | | Frame indexing and count | Preserved | | Denominator and rounding | Unchanged | | Ownership producer | Unchanged | | Motion preprocessing | Unchanged | | Grid construction | Unchanged | | Public signatures and return types | Unchanged | --- ## Local prototype feasibility evidence The disposable prototype modified only `floodlight/models/space.py`. Production diff: ```text 12 additions 0 removals 1 new private symbol 0 new public symbols ``` Results: - 174/174 assigned-frame outputs were exactly identical - 0 assigned frames changed - all 18 fully missing model/mesh results changed from zero to `NaN` - all fully missing frames remained retained and aligned - all 90 one-team and partial-dropout comparisons remained exactly unchanged - all 18 empty-team boundary combinations gained no new exception or shape regression - focused tests: 66/66 passed - existing space-control tests: 18/18 passed - all model tests: 134/134 passed - downstream temporal/zone tests: 28/28 passed - complete repository suite: 345/345 passed - Black, Flake8, and `git diff --check` passed A controlled mutation replaced the four `NaN` assignments with `0.0`. All 12 selected missing-output regression tests failed on the intended assertions. Restoring `NaN` caused all 12 to pass again. The prototype was not committed, pushed, or proposed for merge. --- ## Solution directions considered These directions address different contracts. They are not equivalent implementations of the same repair. | Direction | Problem addressed | Additional state or API | Maintenance surface | Proposed status | |---|---|---|---|---| | No-owner `NaN` guard | Fully undefined ownership becomes numeric zero | Existing ownership grid only | Low | Recommended initial PR | | One-team observation guard | Missing opposition becomes `100/0` | Retained input-observation state | Medium | Separate policy discussion | | Observation-quality sidecar | Missingness is not publicly communicated | New metadata/public lifecycle | High initially | Separate RFC/design issue | | Finite-owner denominator | Attempts to exclude undefined cells | Formula change | Adds little value | Rejected | | Motion-support validity | Derivatives depend on missing neighboring frames | Velocity-stencil support state | Separate contract | Follow-up design | ### Recommended: no-owner `NaN` guard Advantages: - repairs the only categorically undefined public output; - uses the missing state already preserved internally; - requires no new public interface or retained input state; - leaves every assigned frame unchanged; - applies consistently to all models and meshes; - has a small, testable, shared implementation boundary. Limitations are deliberate: one-team dropout remains `100/0`, partial-player dropout remains conditional, and motion derivative support remains undisclosed. ### Broader policy alternative: one-team observation guard A stronger policy could require at least one observed player from each team. Potentially, if either team is entirely unobserved, all player and team outputs for that frame would become `NaN`. Scientific advantage: - prevents missing-opposition `100/0` from appearing as a complete tactical estimate. Maintenance and compatibility cost: - percentages alone cannot distinguish legitimate complete `100/0` from missing-team `100/0`; - input-observation state must be retained or propagated from `fit()`; - deliberately one-sided inputs and tracking dropout need distinct semantics; - existing one-team behavior changes; - broader player/team consistency rules are required. The experiment strongly motivates this discussion, but the policy belongs to maintainers and should not be combined silently with the narrow repair. ### Longer-term API alternative: observation-quality sidecar Potential information could include: ```text position_observation_status observed_home_players observed_away_players home_observed_fraction away_observed_fraction both_teams_observed motion_support_valid ``` Advantages: - communicates incomplete observation without automatically discarding every conditional estimate; - distinguishes per-team observation completeness; - can separately disclose position presence and derivative support. Design and maintenance cost: - requires a new public contract; - may affect slicing, copying, resampling, pandas conversion, serialization, plotting, and downstream consumers; - counts and fractions are identity-blind and insufficient as validity criteria; - overall coverage hides team asymmetry; - owned-cell fraction is degenerate; - one flat enum may be insufficient. At least three independent dimensions may coexist: ```text position-observation completeness temporal missingness pattern motion-derivative support ``` This is better treated as a separate RFC or design issue. ### Rejected: finite-owned-cell denominator Replacing `owned count / all cells` with `owned count / finite owner cells` was rejected because the current producer normally assigns every grid cell whenever any valid player remains. Consequently, it does not detect one-team or partial-player dropout, still returns a conserved conditional 100% partition, changes the aggregation formula, and produces missingness for the fully undefined case only indirectly through a zero denominator. The explicit no-owner guard communicates the intended semantics more clearly and with less technical debt. ### Separate contract: motion-support validity Position observation and derivative support are not the same state. Taki–Hasegawa and Fujimura–Sugihara may depend on missing coordinates in neighboring frames even when the current frame's positions are finite. A future motion-support field requires a precise definition of derivative-stencil support, potentially at player rather than frame level. This should not be solved by changing or interpolating velocities in this proposal. ---
Adjacent findings intentionally excluded from the initial repair The investigation also reproduced or identified adjacent technical contracts: - half-missing coordinate pairs can bypass the full-frame skip and raise an all-`NaN` reduction error; - empty teams can produce a malformed empty player-property shape `(0,)`; - exact ownership ties favor the first stacked player identifier; - input validation is permissive for sequence lengths, framerates, coordinate pairs, and empty teams; - motion-model missingness can affect neighboring valid frames. These findings are not required to repair fully no-owner aggregation semantics and should not be combined into the initial PR without explicit maintainer agreement.
--- ## Historical context The all-cell aggregation behavior was introduced before Floodlight began preserving all-`NaN` ownership frames. A later change taught the ownership producer to skip completely missing frames and retain their internal `NaN` state, but the public player/team aggregators were not updated to preserve that missingness. The current `0/0` behavior therefore appears likely incidental rather than an explicitly documented missing-output policy. --- ## Why the proposed initial scope remains narrow The broader findings do not weaken the no-owner repair. They explain why it should not silently define unrelated policy. The proposed initial PR would address only: ```text no assigned owner exists → expose NaN for every player and both teams ``` It would not decide one-team-only policy, partial-player semantics, observation metadata, motion derivative support, or malformed-input validation. Those questions have materially different state, API, and maintenance requirements and should become separate follow-up issues or an RFC after maintainer feedback. --- ## Explicit exclusions The proposed initial repair would not: - change one-team or partial-dropout behavior; - change motion or velocity preprocessing; - add observation-quality metadata; - add or change public method signatures; - change `PlayerProperty` or `TeamProperty`; - validate half-missing coordinate pairs; - repair empty-team output shapes; - change exact-tie behavior; - change percentage denominators or rounding; - change mesh generation or model equations; - interpolate missing positions; - omit frames. --- ## Proposed acceptance criteria - no-owner frames remain temporally aligned; - every retained player and both teams are `NaN` on no-owner frames; - every assigned-frame player and team output remains exactly unchanged; - player and team aggregation share one private no-owner rule; - all three models and both mesh types are covered; - valid/missing/valid sequences preserve order and adjacent valid output; - one-team and partial-dropout behavior is not changed; - empty-team behavior is not worsened; - output classes, normal shapes, names, and framerate remain unchanged; - no public API, denominator, rounding, producer, motion, grid, or tie-policy change is introduced; - focused tests and the complete suite pass; - lint and `git diff --check` pass; - regression tests fail if `NaN` is replaced with zero. --- ## Maintainer questions 1. Should a frame with no assigned owner expose `NaN` for every player and both team-control outputs instead of numeric zero? 2. Is the aggregation-only no-owner guard an acceptable scope for an initial PR? 3. Should one-team observation policy and observation-quality metadata remain separate follow-up discussions? 4. Is a changelog entry expected for this numerical missingness correction? 5. Are there known downstream compatibility expectations for fully unobserved space-control frames that the eventual PR should preserve?   "body": "## Summary\n\nStatsBomb records the team performing an event separately from the team in possession.\n\nFloodlight currently selects the destination team-specific `Events` container from `possession_team`, while the event row's existing `tID` is populated from the acting `team`. Defensive actions can therefore be stored in the opponent's `Events` object even though their rows identify the defending team.\n\nThis change selects the destination container from the acting team so that container ownership and row `tID` agree.\n\nPossession information remains unchanged and continues to be preserved in the event qualifier.\n\n## What changed\n\nThe StatsBomb parser now resolves the destination Home/Away container using `event[\"team\"][\"id\"]` instead of `event[\"possession_team\"][\"id\"]`.\n\nNo event fields, possession values, clock calculations, coordinate handling, segment logic, or StatsBomb 360 enrichment were changed.\n\n## Regression coverage\n\nThe synthetic regression covers:\n\n- an attacking agreement case where acting team and possession team are Team A;\n- defensive disagreement cases where Team B performs events during Team A possession;\n- presence and absence in both team-specific `Events` containers;\n- agreement between container ownership and row `tID`;\n- total event-count preservation;\n- source-relative event ordering within the corrected acting-team streams;\n- event IDs, types, players, outcomes, timestamps, clocks, coordinates, and qualifiers;\n- possession metadata preservation;\n- StatsBomb 360 freeze-frame and visible-area preservation.\n\nThe regression fails against the previous implementation specifically because the Team B defensive event is stored in Team A's possession-owned container.\n\nA mutation restoring possession-team ownership is also detected by the regression.\n\n## Behavioral compatibility\n\nThis is an intentional behavioral correction.\n\nTeam-specific event membership and counts change when an event's acting team differs from its possession team. Total event count, row contents, and return-object structure remain unchanged.\n\nFor malformed records, container resolution now follows the acting-team mapping rather than the possession-team mapping. As a consequence:\n\n- a missing or unknown `possession_team` no longer prevents parsing when the acting team maps successfully;\n- a missing or unknown acting-team ID fails through the existing Home/Away lookup.\n\nNo fallback, new public exceptional-record policy, or public API change is introduced.\n\n## Validation\n\n- Focused regression: `1 passed`\n- StatsBomb test module: `2 passed`\n- Full test suite: `280 passed`\n- CI-equivalent coverage suite: `280 passed`\n- Pre-commit: passed\n- `git diff --check`: passed\n- Possession-selector mutation: killed\n- Independent semantic parser probe: passed\n\n## Scope\n\nAddresses the event-team attribution portion of #135.\n\nThis contribution does not modify:\n\n- event or frame clocks;\n- segment-relative time behavior;\n- source loading or local-file discovery;\n- StatsBomb API or `statsbombpy` integration;\n- possession semantics;\n- coordinate handling;\n- event taxonomy;\n- StatsBomb 360 behavior;\n- other provider parsers.\n",

import csv
import json
import math
import os
import random
import time
import numpy as np
import pulp as plp
import multiprocessing as mp
import pandas as pd
import statistics
import itertools
import collections
import re
import warnings
from tqdm import tqdm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy.stats import norm, kendalltau, multivariate_normal, gamma
import numba as nb
from random import shuffle

@nb.jit(nopython=True)  # nopython mode ensures the function is fully optimized
def salary_boost(salary, max_salary):
    return (salary / max_salary) ** 2
    
def create_dummy_pitcher():
    # Create a default pitcher with average or placeholder stats
    return {
        "ID": "dummy",
        "Fpts": 1, 
        "StdDev": 1,  
        "Name": "Justin Case",
        "Position": ["P"],
    }

def format_lineup_dk(lu_names, lineup, fpts_p, ceil_p, salary, win_p, Top1Percent_p, roi_p, own_p, roi_round, stacks, hitters_vs_pitcher, lu_type, simDupes):
    return "{} ({}),{} ({}),{} ({}),{} ({}),{} ({}),{} ({}),{} ({}),{} ({}),{} ({}),{} ({}),{},{},${},{}%,{}%,{}%,{},${},{},{},{},{},{}".format(
        lu_names[0].replace("#", "-"), lineup[0],
        lu_names[1].replace("#", "-"), lineup[1],
        lu_names[2].replace("#", "-"), lineup[2],
        lu_names[3].replace("#", "-"), lineup[3],
        lu_names[4].replace("#", "-"), lineup[4],
        lu_names[5].replace("#", "-"), lineup[5],
        lu_names[6].replace("#", "-"), lineup[6],
        lu_names[7].replace("#", "-"), lineup[7],
        lu_names[8].replace("#", "-"), lineup[8],
        lu_names[9].replace("#", "-"), lineup[9],
        fpts_p, ceil_p, salary, win_p, Top1Percent_p, roi_p, own_p, roi_round,
        str(stacks[0][0]) + " " + str(stacks[0][1]),
        str(stacks[1][0]) + " " + str(stacks[1][1]),
        hitters_vs_pitcher, lu_type, simDupes
    )

def format_lineup_fd(lu_names, lineup, fpts_p, ceil_p, salary, win_p, Top1Percent_p, roi_p, own_p, roi_round, stacks, hitters_vs_pitcher, lu_type, simDupes):
    return "{}:{},{}:{},{}:{},{}:{},{}:{},{}:{},{}:{},{}:{},{}:{},{},{},{},{}%,{}%,{}%,{},${},{},{},{},{},{}".format(
        lineup[0], lu_names[0].replace("#", "-"),
        lineup[1], lu_names[1].replace("#", "-"),
        lineup[2], lu_names[2].replace("#", "-"),
        lineup[3], lu_names[3].replace("#", "-"),
        lineup[4], lu_names[4].replace("#", "-"),
        lineup[5], lu_names[5].replace("#", "-"),
        lineup[6], lu_names[6].replace("#", "-"),
        lineup[7], lu_names[7].replace("#", "-"),
        lineup[8], lu_names[8].replace("#", "-"),
        fpts_p, ceil_p, salary, win_p, Top1Percent_p, roi_p, own_p, roi_round,
        str(stacks[0][0]) + " " + str(stacks[0][1]),
        str(stacks[1][0]) + " " + str(stacks[1][1]),
        hitters_vs_pitcher, lu_type, simDupes
    )

def format_lineup_ikb(lu_names, lineup, fpts_p, ceil_p, salary, win_p, Top1Percent_p, roi_p, own_p, roi_round, stacks, hitters_vs_pitcher, lu_type, simDupes):
    return "{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},{},${},{}%,{}%,{}%,${},${},{},{},{},{},{}".format(
        lineup[0], lineup[1], lineup[2], lineup[3], lineup[4], lineup[5], lineup[6], lineup[7], lineup[8], lineup[9],
        lu_names[0].replace("#", "-"), lu_names[1].replace("#", "-"), lu_names[2].replace("#", "-"), lu_names[3].replace("#", "-"),
        lu_names[4].replace("#", "-"), lu_names[5].replace("#", "-"), lu_names[6].replace("#", "-"), lu_names[7].replace("#", "-"),
        lu_names[8].replace("#", "-"), lu_names[9].replace("#", "-"),
        fpts_p, ceil_p, salary, win_p, Top1Percent_p, roi_p, own_p, roi_round,
        str(stacks[0][0]) + " " + str(stacks[0][1]), str(stacks[1][0]) + " " + str(stacks[1][1]),
        hitters_vs_pitcher, lu_type, simDupes
    )

class MLB_GPP_Simulator:
    config = None
    player_dict = {}
    field_lineups = {}
    gen_lineup_list = []
    roster_construction = []
    salary = None
    optimal_score = None
    field_size = None
    team_list = []
    num_iterations = None
    site = None
    payout_structure = {}
    use_contest_data = False
    cut_event = False
    entry_fee = None
    use_lineup_input = None
    max_hitters_per_team = None
    matchups = set()
    projection_minimum = 15
    randomness_amount = 100
    min_lineup_salary = 48000
    max_pct_off_optimal = 0.4
    seen_lineups = {}
    seen_lineups_ix = {}
    game_info = {}
    allow_opps = False
    id_name_dict = {}
    stacks_dict = {}

    def __init__(
        self,
        site,
        field_size,
        num_iterations,
        use_contest_data,
        use_lineup_input,
        match_lineup_input_to_field_size,
    ):
        self.site = site
        self.max_stack_len = 5 if site == 'dk' else 4
        self.use_lineup_input = use_lineup_input
        self.match_lineup_input_to_field_size = match_lineup_input_to_field_size
        self.load_config()
        self.load_rules()

        projection_path = os.path.join(
            os.path.dirname(__file__),
            "../{}_data/{}".format(site, self.config["projection_path"]),
        )
        self.load_projections(projection_path)

        player_path = os.path.join(
            os.path.dirname(__file__),
            "../{}_data/{}".format(site, self.config["player_path"]),
        )
        self.load_player_ids(player_path)

        stacks_path = os.path.join(
            os.path.dirname(__file__),

    def get_optimal(self):
        #for p, s in self.player_dict.items():
        #    print(p, s["ID"])

        problem = plp.LpProblem("MLB", plp.LpMaximize)
        lp_variables = {
            self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]: plp.LpVariable(
                str(self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]), cat="Binary"
            )
            for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
        }

        # for key, v in lp_variables.items():
        #     print(key, v)

        # set the objective - maximize fpts
        problem += (
            plp.lpSum(
                self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["fieldFpts"]
                * lp_variables[self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]]
                for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
            ),
            "Objective",
        )

        # Set the salary constraints
        problem += (
            plp.lpSum(
                self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["Salary"]
                * lp_variables[self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]]
                for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
            )
            <= self.salary
        )

        if self.site == "dk":
            # Need 2 pitchers
            problem += (
                plp.lpSum(
                    lp_variables[self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]]
                    for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
                    if "P" in self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["Position"]
                )
                == 2
            )
            # Need 1 catcher
            problem += (
                plp.lpSum(
                    lp_variables[self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]]
                    for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
                    if "C" in self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["Position"]
                )
                == 1
            )
            # Need 1 first baseman
            problem += (
                plp.lpSum(
                    lp_variables[self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]]
                    for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
                    if "1B" in self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["Position"]
                )
                == 1
            )
            # Need at least 1 power forward, can have up to 3 if utilizing F and UTIL slots
            problem += (
                plp.lpSum(
                    lp_variables[self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]]
                    for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
                    if "2B" in self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["Position"]
                )

            )
            # Need at least 1 center, can have up to 2 if utilizing C and UTIL slots
            problem += (
                plp.lpSum(

                    for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict

            problem += (

                    for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
                    if "SS" in self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["Position"]
                )
                == 1
            )
            # Need 3 outfielders
            problem += (
                plp.lpSum(
                    lp_variables[self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["ID"]]
                    for (player, pos_str, team) in self.player_dict
                    if "OF" in self.player_dict[(player, pos_str, team)]["Position"]

            )
            # Can only roster 8 total players

    @staticmethod
    def adjust_probabilities(salaries, ownership, salary_ceiling):
